reason: Leaf teeth can be sharp. The examples describe the tooth tip, so the reading is correct.
Spathes and similar flat organs have a 2-D shape (ovate, elliptic). The part is an anatomy class and the examples are correct. Orbicular in cross section also fits 2-D shape.
A calyx tube can be subglobose, and subglobose maps to a spheroid shape.
Isodiametric cells are cells of equal dimensions, which is isometrical. PATO marks it as a cell quality.
Ligulate or linguiform organs are strap-shaped. Lips, lobes and petals can have this shape.
Leaf blades and margins can be curled. Curling of a blade tip is a looser reading, but it is still correct for the blade.
Colour is meaningful for glochids and tufts, which are anatomy classes. The examples are colour terms, apart from the word tuft.
A rhizome can grow obliquely, which is a growth orientation.

Height fits a corona or a gynostegium. But the examples include '2–3.5 × 4–5 cm', where the numbers are length and width, not height. A rule would need to check whether the text says high, tall or height, and not accept bare measurements.
Spathe apices can be acute, acuminate and so on. PATO sharpness has the synonym apiculate and is used for apex shape.
Scale leaf and cataphyll apices can be acute.
Auriculate bases occur on leaves, bracts and similar organs. The examples describe the base correctly.
Secondary veins can be straight or curved, and this is a standard venation character.
A lobe can be longer than its neighbours (relative length). The examples such as '15–34 cm long' are plain measurements. These should be a length value, not an increased length.
Nuts have a surface pattern (reticulate, cancellate). The examples are correct. Cases of 'not reticulate' are negations and need negation handling.
Tubes, bases and other organs can be curved.
Perianth parts and similar organs can be hairy. Terms like puberulent, villous and strigose are kinds of hairiness.
Width is meaningful for any flat or elongate organ. The examples are correct width measurements.

'Present' fits when the veins are mentioned as present. But 'numerous' is a count, '2 mm apart' is a spacing, and the example 'lateral' has no quality. A rule would need to separate presence from number and spacing.
Lateral veins can be arched, which is a standard venation character.

The examples are 'apex acute' and French 'très aiguës' with no trichome in them. They may belong to leaves or other organs in the same sentence. A trichome tip can be sharp. A rule would need the bearer to be named in the same clause.
A perigynium can be sessile or stipitate, and this is used to tell Carex species apart.
Hairs can be straight or curved.
Reticulate patterns apply to surfaces and to fruit or seed coats. The examples are correct.
Membranous and fibrous describe the bulb tunic (outer scales), not the whole bulb. A rule would need to map to the tunic or the outer scale part.
Sepals can have a blunt apex. 'Hood narrowly rounded' is borderline but acceptable.

'Bracts few' is a count of the bract itself. The PATO term 'has fewer parts of type' fits a part with fewer sub-parts. It is the wrong reading unless the number belongs to the parent, such as an inflorescence. A rule would need to attach 'few' to the parent.
Sides can be plane or eroded. These are shape terms and the examples are fine.
The wings of an inflorescence axis have a width. The examples are about wings, so the bearer is a bit loose, but the pair is meaningful.
Heads have a rounded 3-D shape such as hemispheric, globose or ovoid.
Ovaries can be lanate or woolly.
Leaf sheaths can be glossy, and PATO glistening has glossy as a synonym.
A ligule can be fimbriate (fringed).
Disks can be cushion-shaped (pulvinate). The examples agree.
Achenes can be quadrangular (4-angled), including in French.
Width of an organ. The examples are correct.

The examples say 'outside striped', so the stripes are on a different organ, such as the perianth or corolla. They come from one flora. A rule would need the bearer, not the ligule, to carry the stripes.
Legumes can be straight or curved. 'Nervure rectiligne' is a vein, so a rule is needed for that example.
A fertile lemma can have a colour.
A style head has a length, and the examples are correct.
Drupelets are listed as present. This reading is fine, though the examples are mostly mentions with no quality.
Margins and similar parts can be membranous or scarious, which is texture.
Sporangia can be present or absent. The examples such as 'apiculum 0-1.3 mm' are not about presence, so some noise remains.
Surfaces can be hairy or glabrous. The adaxial and abaxial qualifiers need separate handling.
Abaxial leaf surfaces can be sericeous.
Organs, bases and veins can be thickened. This is a plain quality and the examples are correct.
An awn can be short.
Thorns and spines have an orientation (ascending, spreading).
A petiole can be spreading.
The examples include 'glaucous', which is a wax bloom and not a colour. The colour examples are fine. A rule would need to route glaucous to its own term.
Capsules can be horizontal, which is an orientation.
A leaflet can be filiform. But some examples are 'filiform tail', which belongs to the tail or tip. A rule would need to attach the quality to the tail.
Stipules can be setose (bristly).
A petiolule can be spiny or prickly.
Width of an organ. Some examples are 'length × width' pairs, but the width part is correct.
A disk can be cylindrical.
Dimidiate and asymmetrical bases or blades are asymmetry, a standard leaf character.
Scale leaves and cataphylls can be lanceolate.
Irregular is used for pollen shape and also for irregular size. The examples say 'irregular in size', which is a size variation and not a spatial pattern. A rule would need to tell shape from size.
A glume can be amplexicaul (clasping the spikelet base).
